newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE-Sulky France to vote amid disenchantment.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Sulky France to vote amid disenchantment.

text.p: A gloomy France votes in the first round of a parliamentary election next Sunday disenchanted with both major blocs and sceptical about President Jacques Chirac's reasons for calling the vote 10 months early.

Opinion polls suggest his ruling centre-right coalition will be re-elected with a sharply reduced majority, but two-thirds of voters do not want him to reappoint Prime Minister Alain Juppe, widely blamed for austerity, record unemployment and high taxes.
"France is sulking," the weekly magazine L'Express headlined a cover story on the national mood.

Surveys show most voters are deeply dissatisfied by the way the country is governed, do not trust either the coalition's or the Socialist-Communist opposition's platforms and doubt the election will make any difference to their lives.

Juppe has felt obliged to warn conservative voters against the temptation of abstaining or casting protest votes for the extreme-right National Front and dissident candidates, though the two-round voting system in single-member constituencies means they will win few, if any seats.
VOTERS DISENCHANTED WITH CHIRAC'S RECORD

Two years after Chirac was elected promising an all-out war on unemployment, the jobless rate has inched up from 11.7 percent to a postwar record of 12.8 percent, the highest in any major industrialised democracy.
Almost one young person in four under the age of 25 is unemployed despite a thicket of job-creation subsidies.
Economic growth has been sluggish, purchasing power is stagnant and the tax burden hit a record 45.7 percent of gross domestic product last year.
Polls show a majority of voters feel Chirac has broken his election promises and do not believe the centre-right's pledges of cuts in payroll charges and taxation to create jobs.
Few believe government assurances that a single European currency will stimulate growth and employment, and many fear it may mean permanent austerity.

Nor do they trust the Socialists' pledge to create 700,000 youth jobs, half of them in the public sector, and cut the working week to 35 hours from 39 without loss of pay, let alone the Communists' proposal to raise the minimum wage by 1,000 francs ($200) a month to stimulate demand.
MITTERRAND LEGACY HOBBLES SOCIALISTS

Despite Socialist leader Lionel Jospin's efforts to give his party a new face, many voters have not forgiven the Socialists for the stagnation and sleaze of the late president Francois Mitterrand's last years in power, which led to a centre-right landslide in the 1993 parliamentary election.
Recent disclosures that Mitterrand personally supervised the telephone tapping of journalists, lawyers and politicians in the mid-1980s have embarrassed the Socialists.
For a moment at the start of the campaign, it seemed France might be given a sharp choice between a radical, deregulating right and a Keynesian redistributive left.

But the lines have since blurred, although political analyst Alain Duhamel noted the policy divide is wider than between the U.S. Republicans and Democrats, or Britain's Conservative and Labour parties.
Chirac and Juppe made clear they were not proposing a bold, Thatcherite rolling back of the frontiers of the state but a gradual, cautious slimming down of big government.
FRENCH CLING TO PROTECTIVE STATE
The reason was clear. Opinion research showed a majority of voters want a strong, protective state and are profoundly attached to the costly public health and welfare system.

"Whenever there is a problem in France, people turn to the state," lamented Rene Monory, the centre-right Senate speaker, who caused one of the few stirs of the campaign by saying the national minimum wage was bound to disappear.

Coalition spokesmen immediately disowned his comments, given the strong consensus in favour of the 6,400 franc ($1,120) monthly minimum wage, which right-wing economists cite as a major barrier to employment.

Rejecting "laisser faire" and "ultra-liberalism", Chirac and Juppe also sidelined Alain Madelin, the right's leading advocate of raw, free-market economics, who left his chair empty when Juppe presented the coalition's programme.
Instead, the ruling duo seem to offer a continuation of the policy mix of Chirac's presidential election campaign -- a bit less state and a bit more private enterprise, but no big bang.

"Why call an election and appeal for a new elan if it's to continue the same policies with the same prime minister?" asked Jean-Pierre Maillet, a self-employed businessman in the western town of Poitiers, voicing a widely-expressed sentiment.

On the left, the French Socialists took heart from the May 1 election victory of Britain's Labour party but showed little sign of undergoing the radical conversion to free-market economics which Tony Blair had pushed through his party.
They have promised to halt the planned sell-off of stakes in France Telecom and defence electronics giant Thomson CSF and opposed the privatisation of Air France.
"The right is less liberal and the left is more Socialist in France than elsewhere in Europe. We haven't yet had our cultural revolution," former prime minister Edouard Balladur said.
GOVERNMENT REFORM EFFORTS MET BY STRIKES

Government efforts to shake up the civil service, streamline the loss-making state railways and bring the generous working conditions of French airline staff more into line with lower-cost competitors have been met by strikes.

A 24-day public transport strike in November and December 1995 forced Juppe to drop plans to make civil servants and train drivers work longer for a full pension, although he stuck to unpopular reforms to curb the welfare system's chronic deficit.
Juppe's public standing has never recovered. He briefly became the Fifth Republic's most unpopular prime minister and his approval rating remains below 30 percent.
Even in Chirac's rural home bastion of Correze, in central France, local Gaullists are pleading for a new face.

"Juppe is leading the right to disaster," Bernard Bourguignon, mayor of the village of Sainte-Fortunade, told the Gaullist candidate at an election rally. "Isn't it necessary and indeed indispensible to say he will not be the next premier?"
Unlike in most other European countries, labour unrest often has broad public sympathy in France.
The public was supportive when truck drivers barricaded the nation's highways for 12 days last December to win the right to retire at 55 and improved working conditions.
Since then, train conductors, airline staff, civil servants and bank workers have all staged strikes against attempts to withdraw "acquired rights" or change their working conditions.
Some commentators fear that if Chirac reappoints Juppe, the government could face another big labour protest movement by the end of the year.
